questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: The principal argument for "shifting left" on security is that:
options: Security testing tools only work on source code
Late testing breaches the Privacy Act
Developers prefer to work on security early
The cost of fixing a defect rises exponentially the later in the SDLC it is found
questions.explanation: A flaw caught at the requirements or design phase costs a conversation; the same flaw caught after release costs a patch, a re-test, a deployment, possible notification obligations and reputational damage.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: How many phases are in the Secure SDLC as taught in this course?
questions.explanation: 8 — Requirements → Specifications → Design → Development → Integration → Testing & debugging → Installation → Maintenance, with findings feeding back to the start.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Threat modelling is carried out during which SDLC phase?
questions.explanation: Design — Threat modelling systematically identifies likely attacks against a proposed architecture, so it must happen while the architecture is still a decision rather than a build.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: "Deciding that AES will be used to encrypt medical records at rest" belongs to which phase?
questions.explanation: Determining specifications — choosing which standard, algorithm or method. Writing the code that performs the encryption is Development.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: The classic exam trap between Design and Development is that:
options: Design decides what security features will exist; Development writes the code implementing them
Design writes the code; Development plans it
questions.explanation: Read the described activity carefully — is it planning/deciding or building?

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: "Closing unused ports and removing default credentials on the production server" is which phase?
questions.explanation: Installation — This is system hardening at deployment. Ongoing patching and vulnerability scanning after release is Maintenance.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Combining a trusted in-house login module with a third-party payment component without creating new weaknesses is the security concern of which phase?
questions.explanation: Integration — Two individually secure components can create a vulnerability at the seam — mismatched trust assumptions, unvalidated data crossing the boundary, or excessive data exposure.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Which best describes how end users influence secure design?
options: Users have no effect on security decisions
The technical skill, needs and behaviour of the user group shape which controls are usable and therefore actually effective
questions.explanation: A control users route around is not a control. Elderly or low-literacy users may need an alternative to biometrics; high-security staff may accept hardware tokens that consumers would abandon.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Requiring a complex 16-character password that users then write on a sticky note illustrates:
options: A control that reduces real security because it ignores user behaviour
questions.explanation: Usability and security are not opposites but they interact — a policy so demanding that users defeat it has made the system less secure, not more.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Security by Design's five key principles include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The five are systematic integration, threat modelling and risk assessment, built-in security measures, continuous monitoring and auditing, and a proactive approach. Remediation-only is precisely what Security by Design rejects.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Which triad member is compromised by a successful DDoS attack?
questions.explanation: Availability — A DoS/DDoS does not read or alter data — it prevents authorised users from reaching it. Countermeasures: rate limiting, load balancing, CDN filtering, scalable and redundant design.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: A checksum mismatch on a downloaded file indicates a failure of:
questions.explanation: Integrity — The sender calculates the checksum and sends it with the file; the receiver recalculates and compares. Different values mean the data was altered in transit and the file should be rejected.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: "What can you do once you're logged in?" is the question answered by:
questions.explanation: Authorisation — implemented through RBAC or ACLs. Authentication asks who are you; accountability asks what did you do.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Which control most directly supports accountability?
questions.explanation: Accountability requires a record of who accessed or modified what, and when — implemented with audit tables, secure logging and SIEM monitoring.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: MFA is described as the single most effective control against broken authentication because:
options: A stolen password alone is no longer sufficient to gain access
It removes the need for passwords
questions.explanation: MFA combines something you know, have or are, so credential stuffing and brute force become far less effective even when the password is known.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: In RBAC, giving an "Editor" the ability to create and edit content but not to delete it is an example of:
questions.explanation: RBAC assigns permissions by job role rather than to individuals, and access rights must be regularly reviewed as roles change.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Confidentiality is best achieved through:
options: Encryption plus access control so only authorised individuals can read the data
questions.explanation: Redundancy and failover serve availability; checksums and version control serve integrity.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Which pairing is correct?
options: Availability → redundancy and failover · Integrity → hashing and version control
questions.explanation: Availability = redundancy, failover, backups, scalable design. Integrity = checksums, hashing, version control, secure coding preventing injection.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Non-repudiation means:
options: The message was not altered in transit
Only authorised users can read the message
The sender cannot later deny having sent or signed the message
The system remains available under load
questions.explanation: Provided by digital signatures — only the holder of the private key could have produced the signature. Distinct from integrity (unaltered) and authentication (identity).

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: A hospital system must ensure that a patient record is accurate and unmodified, only visible to treating staff, and reachable during a power failure. Which triad members are engaged, in that order?
questions.explanation: Accurate and unmodified = Integrity; visible only to treating staff = Confidentiality; reachable during a failure = Availability.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: The key difference between encryption and hashing is that:
options: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is one-way and cannot be reversed
Encryption is one-way; hashing is reversible
Hashing requires a public and private key pair
questions.explanation: Passwords should be hashed (never decrypted, only compared); data that must be read later must be encrypted.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Salting defeats which specific attack?
questions.explanation: Rainbow tables — Adding random data unique to each user before hashing means two users with the same password produce different hashes, so a precomputed hash table is useless.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: AES supports key sizes of:
questions.explanation: 128, 192 or 256 bits — AES is symmetric — one key encrypts and decrypts — and is the standard choice for data at rest.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Which statement about asymmetric encryption is correct?
options: The public key encrypts and the private key decrypts, making it suited to data in transit and digital signatures
One shared key both encrypts and decrypts
It is faster than symmetric encryption for bulk data
It cannot be used with TLS
questions.explanation: Asymmetric solves the key-distribution problem but is computationally expensive, which is why TLS uses it only to agree a shared symmetric key.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: During the TLS handshake, asymmetric encryption is used to:
options: Verify the certificate and agree a shared symmetric key, after which fast symmetric encryption carries the session
questions.explanation: Browser requests a secure connection → server sends its certificate → browser verifies it against a trusted CA → asymmetric exchange establishes a session key → symmetric encryption for speed.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: A Certificate Authority exists to:
options: Issue and sign certificates so a browser can confirm a server is who it claims to be
questions.explanation: Encryption alone stops eavesdropping; the certificate stops impersonation — together they defeat a man-in-the-middle attack.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: In chr((ord(char) - 97 + shift) % 26 + 97), the value 97 is used because:
options: It is the maximum shift allowed
It is the ASCII value of lowercase 'a', converting to a 0-based alphabet index
It is the ASCII value of 'A'
questions.explanation: ord('a') = 97 and ord('A') = 65. Subtracting gives a 0–25 index, % 26 wraps around the alphabet, then adding it back returns to ASCII.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Applying a Caesar cipher with a shift of 3 to "HELLO" produces:
questions.explanation: "KHOOR" — Each letter shifts forward three positions: H→K, E→H, L→O, L→O, O→R.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: A digital signature is produced by signing data with the:
questions.explanation: Sender's private key — , and verified with their public key. This proves authenticity and integrity and provides non-repudiation.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Encryption at rest and in transit are best described as:
options: At rest protects stored data, usually with symmetric encryption such as AES; in transit protects data crossing a network, using TLS
At rest uses TLS; in transit uses AES
Only data in transit needs protection
questions.explanation: A complete answer to "how would you protect this data" covers both — encrypting the database is useless if the login form posts over plain HTTP.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Fernet in Python's cryptography library provides:
options: Symmetric authenticated cryptography — the same key encrypts and decrypts
questions.explanation: It generates a URL-safe base64-encoded 32-byte key. For password storage you would use bcrypt, not Fernet — passwords should be hashed, not encrypted.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: An HSM and a KMS both address:
options: Secure storage and management of encryption keys
questions.explanation: An HSM is dedicated hardware; a KMS (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS) is a cloud service. Both exist because a key hard-coded in source is not a secret.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Which of the following is not symmetric?
questions.explanation: RSA — is asymmetric (public/private key pair). AES, DES and Fernet are symmetric.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: A checksum can detect that a file was altered but cannot:
options: Prove who altered it or prevent the alteration
questions.explanation: A checksum is an integrity detection mechanism. Attribution needs digital signatures and logging; prevention needs access control.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Plaintext is:
options: The encrypted, unreadable form of data
questions.explanation: Ciphertext is the encrypted form. Encryption converts plaintext → ciphertext; decryption reverses it with the key.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: The three purposes of sandboxing are:
questions.explanation: Isolation (a controlled environment separate from the main system) · testing (safely trial new software) · security (contain malware). Examples: separate browser tab processes, antivirus opening a suspicious file in a VM, app permission prompts, VMs and containers.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Containerisation (e.g. Docker) is best described as:
options: Packaging an application with everything it needs to run in an isolated environment
questions.explanation: It is sandboxing at whole-application level, which also makes environments reproducible between development and production.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: The three syllabus principles of Privacy by Design are:
options: Proactive not reactive · embedded into design · respect for user privacy
questions.explanation: The class notes give the full Cavoukian seven, adding privacy as the default setting, positive-sum, end-to-end lifecycle security, and visibility and transparency. Answer with the three, then add "privacy as the default" and "end-to-end protection" as extra depth on a 5+ mark question.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Replacing an exact age with a range such as "30–35" is which anonymisation technique?
questions.explanation: Generalisation — reducing precision. The five techniques are masking, pseudonymisation, generalisation, perturbation (adding noise) and aggregation (reporting averages).

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Data minimisation requires that:
options: Only the data required for the software's stated purpose is collected
questions.explanation: It reduces both privacy exposure and breach impact — data you never collected cannot leak. It is a core Privacy by Design measure.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: If an organisation wants to use collected data for a purpose other than the one it was collected for, it must first:
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation is one of the APPs — use and disclosure is restricted to the purpose for which the data was collected unless fresh consent is obtained.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: How many Australian Privacy Principles are there?
questions.explanation: 13 — , under the Privacy Act 1988. In outline: open and transparent management, collection for a legitimate purpose, use/disclosure limited to that purpose, rights of access and correction, and reasonable steps to keep data secure.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Under the NDB scheme, an organisation must notify:
options: Affected individuals and the OAIC, where the breach is likely to cause serious harm
questions.explanation: "Notify" is the third step of the four-step breach response — Contain → Assess → Notify → Review.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: PCI-DSS applies to:
options: Any system handling payment card data
questions.explanation: GDPR covers EU residents' data; the Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 (NSW) covers NSW health records; the ASD Essential Eight is the Australian baseline mitigation set.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Which is an Australian compliance framework named in the school notes?
questions.explanation: ASD Essential Eight — The full list also includes the Privacy Act 1988, NDB scheme, Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 (NSW), Australian Consumer Law, GDPR, AS/NZS ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002, and the TOLA Act 2018. Naming two or three specific instruments beats "privacy laws".

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: Business continuity differs from disaster recovery because continuity:
options: Keeps critical functions running during and immediately after the disruption
questions.explanation: Continuity = automatic failover so customers barely notice. Disaster recovery = rebuilding and restoring from backups after the event.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: An organisation states that it can tolerate at most one hour of lost data. This is its:
questions.explanation: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — maximum acceptable data loss, which sets backup frequency. RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: A failover system:
options: Requires manual intervention to switch over
Is a type of penetration test
Automatically switches to a standby system when the primary fails, minimising downtime
questions.explanation: It minimises downtime, enhances reliability and ensures continuity — the availability control most directly linked to business continuity.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: The five steps of incident response are:
questions.explanation: The four-step breach response taught alongside it is Contain → Assess → Notify → Review.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: SAST differs from DAST because SAST:
options: Analyses source code, bytecode or binaries without executing the program
Tests a running application from the outside
questions.explanation: The tell in a question is whether the code is executed. SAST finds issues early but generates false positives; DAST finds runtime issues but cannot point to the offending line.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: Bombarding a running application with large volumes of random or malformed input is:
questions.explanation: Fuzzing — a form of dynamic testing performed alongside DAST, used to trigger crashes that reveal unhandled input paths.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: The difference between a vulnerability assessment and a penetration test is that a vulnerability assessment:
options: Actively exploits weaknesses to prove impact
Identifies, quantifies and ranks weaknesses without exploiting them
Is performed after the pen test
questions.explanation: Assessment finds and ranks; penetration testing actively exploits. A pen test is realistic and deep but costly and only a snapshot in time.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: A stated limitation of code review is that:
options: It is time-consuming on large codebases and reviewers may miss subtle issues
It requires the application to be running
questions.explanation: Its strengths are human insight, early detection and knowledge sharing — and crucially it should be done by developers other than the author.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: Which testing strategy would be used earliest in development?
questions.explanation: SAST — it needs only source code, so it runs from the first commits. DAST, fuzzing and pen testing all require something deployed and running.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: Hardening a system involves:
options: Reducing the attack surface — patching, removing unnecessary services, least privilege, firewall configuration, removing default accounts
questions.explanation: The attack surface is the total set of points at which an unauthorised user could try to enter or extract data; hardening shrinks it.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Validation and sanitisation differ because validation:
options: Transforms the input into a safe form
Rejects input that does not meet the expected format, type or range
questions.explanation: Validation rejects; sanitisation transforms (stripping or escaping harmful content). This distinction is directly examinable.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Stripping <script> tags from a submitted comment is:
questions.explanation: Sanitisation — the input is cleaned and accepted rather than rejected. In a PWA, DOMPurify does exactly this before content reaches the DOM.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: The most effective defence against SQL injection is:
options: Client-side validation of the login form
A parameterised query, so user input is treated strictly as data and never as command syntax
Hiding the database server behind a firewall
questions.explanation: WHERE username = ? with the value bound separately. Client-side validation is trivially bypassed, and a firewall does not change how the query is parsed.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: The input ' OR '1'='1 in a login field is an attempt at:
questions.explanation: SQL injection — It closes the string literal and appends a condition that is always true, so the WHERE clause matches every row.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Good error handling in a secure application means:
options: Displaying the full stack trace so users can report it accurately
Showing generic messages to users while logging full detail internally
questions.explanation: Detailed errors leak schema names, file paths and framework versions — free reconnaissance for an attacker. Minimal messages deny them that information.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Whitelisting is generally safer than blacklisting because:
options: It works only on file uploads
It permits only explicitly approved input and fails closed, whereas a blacklist is always incomplete
questions.explanation: A new attack string is not yet on any denylist. Whitelisting aligns with deny by default and least privilege.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Which principle should govern what a public API endpoint returns?
options: Return the full record so the client has flexibility
Least privilege — return only the fields the client actually needs
Return data only over HTTP for speed
Return data unauthenticated to reduce latency
questions.explanation: A public product-listing endpoint should never return the supplier's wholesale cost, even if that field sits in the same table.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: A JWT is used in API design to:
options: Prove a user's identity for a limited time so the password need not be resent with every request
questions.explanation: It supports both authentication (the signed token proves who you are) and session management (it expires, forcing re-authentication).

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Relying solely on client-side validation is unsafe because:
options: It is slower than server-side validation
An attacker can bypass the browser entirely and send crafted requests directly to the API
questions.explanation: Client-side validation is a usability feature. Every input must be validated and sanitised server-side.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Rate limiting on an API primarily prevents:
questions.explanation: It is one of the three load-protection measures, alongside CAPTCHA and load balancing.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Improving session management — limiting session data size and lifetime, expiring idle sessions — benefits:
questions.explanation: Smaller, shorter-lived sessions reduce both the hijacking window and server memory consumption. This link was directly examined in 2025.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Memory management matters for secure, efficient execution because:
options: Memory leaks progressively degrade and eventually crash a system, harming availability
questions.explanation: Buffer overflows — writing past a buffer's bounds — are also a memory-management failure and a classic vulnerability SAST tools scan for.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: In XSS, the attacker's ultimate target is:
options: Other users' browsers, which execute the injected script
questions.explanation: The script is stored or reflected by the site and then runs in victims' browsers, stealing cookies or session tokens. Countermeasures: sanitisation, output encoding, CSP headers.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: In CSRF, the attacker exploits:
options: The victim's existing authenticated session, causing their browser to send a request they did not intend
A buffer overflow in the server
questions.explanation: Countermeasures: CSRF tokens (a unique value per session/form checked on every request), SameSite cookies, and Origin/Referer verification.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: The clearest way to distinguish XSS from CSRF is:
options: XSS affects servers; CSRF affects databases
XSS gets your browser to run their script; CSRF gets your browser to send a request you didn't intend
XSS requires authentication; CSRF does not
questions.explanation: XSS attacks the page; CSRF abuses the session. CSRF specifically requires the victim to be authenticated.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: A request parameter directly names a record ID with no check that the requester owns it. This is:
questions.explanation: IDOR — a form of broken access control and the core vulnerability in the Optus breach. The fix is an ownership/authorisation check on every request, not obscuring the ID.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Redeeming a one-time discount code many times by sending simultaneous requests exploits:
questions.explanation: Race condition — Each request passes the "unused?" check before any request updates the record. Countered by record locking, atomic operations, rate limiting and minimising the check-to-update window.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: An application accepts a user-supplied URL in a redirect parameter. The vulnerability is:
questions.explanation: An attacker crafts a trusted-looking link that lands on a phishing site. Countered by whitelisting permitted destinations and validating redirect targets server-side.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: ../../etc/passwd submitted in a file path field is:
questions.explanation: Path traversal — manipulating a file path to escape the intended directory. Countered by sanitising file names, storing uploads outside the webroot and resolving paths against an allowed base.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Validating an uploaded file by content rather than by extension matters because:
options: An executable can simply be renamed .jpg, so the extension proves nothing
It is required by the APPs
questions.explanation: Also: store uploads outside the webroot, sanitise file names and virus-scan them — because a file the server will execute is a remote code execution risk.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: A login routine that returns "incorrect" the instant it hits a mismatched character is vulnerable to:
questions.explanation: A guess with more correct leading characters takes measurably longer to reject, letting an attacker recover the password one character at a time.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: The countermeasure to a timing attack is an isochronous function, which:
options: Takes the same amount of time regardless of the input, removing the timing signal
Runs faster than a normal comparison
questions.explanation: Supporting measures: generic error messages, randomised delays to add noise, rate limiting, and using well-established cryptographic libraries rather than hand-rolling comparisons.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Broken session management is best countered by:
options: Cryptographically random session IDs, short timeouts and invalidation on logout
questions.explanation: Also: never expose a session ID in a URL — it is bookmarkable, shareable, logged by proxies and directly editable by the user.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Phishing is categorised as a user-action vulnerability because:
options: The software has a coding defect
The software may be entirely sound and the user is the entry point
questions.explanation: Countered by user education, MFA (so a stolen password is insufficient), and email/domain verification — a mix of human and technical controls.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Which is the #1 item in the OWASP Top 10?
questions.explanation: Broken access control — users acting outside intended permissions, e.g. modifying a URL to view another account. Cryptographic failures is #2 and injection #3.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: SSRF is dangerous partly because:
options: It requires physical access to the server
The request originates from inside the trusted network, so it can bypass a firewall, VPN or ACL
questions.explanation: It occurs when an application fetches a remote resource without validating the user-supplied URL, exposing internal services the perimeter was meant to protect.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: "Auto-update functionality that downloads updates without verifying their integrity" is which OWASP category?
questions.explanation: It also covers relying on plugins or libraries from untrusted sources and insecure content-delivery pipelines — supply-chain risk.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Unchanged default passwords and unnecessary open ports fall under:
questions.explanation: Security misconfiguration — default securities not defined or implemented, including overly informative error messages and misconfigured cloud permissions.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Insecure design is distinguished from other OWASP categories because it:
options: Reflects missing security thinking from the beginning, and is difficult to fix once the application is running
questions.explanation: You cannot patch your way out of an architecture that never had a place to put the control. This is the direct argument for Security by Design.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: "Logins and failed logins not logged, no alerting thresholds, pen tests do not trigger alerts" describes:
questions.explanation: The consequence is dwell time — breaches persist undetected for months because nothing was watching, and there is no forensic record afterwards.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: In the 2022 Optus breach, the underlying technical vulnerability was:
options: An unauthenticated API endpoint with directly referenceable customer identifiers
questions.explanation: An IDOR-style exposure on an endpoint that did not authenticate the requester — approximately 9.8 million records were affected.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: The most defensible design lesson from the Optus breach is:
options: Authenticate and authorise every endpoint, apply least privilege to returned fields, and minimise and delete data no longer required
Collect more data to improve detection
questions.explanation: Retention was a major aggravating factor — a large proportion of exposed records belonged to former customers whose data no longer needed to be held.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: A named social/ethical impact of secure software development is digital disruption, meaning:
options: The way the shift to secure, connected software changes industries, business models and communities
questions.explanation: It sits alongside employment, privacy, copyright and intellectual property as the impact considerations for this module.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: In software engineering, copyright most directly governs:
options: Your right to use, modify and redistribute others' code, including open-source licence compliance
questions.explanation: Intellectual property is the broader category, covering ownership of algorithms and novel designs. You must have the right to use a component before shipping it.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: The strongest argument that secure development benefits an enterprise commercially is:
options: It avoids breach costs, regulatory penalties and reputational damage, and builds user trust that is difficult to rebuild once lost
It reduces the number of developers required
It removes the need for testing
questions.explanation: Pair it with the shift-left cost argument for a full-mark answer: cheaper to build securely, and vastly cheaper than the alternative outcome.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: A school portal stores student medical conditions. Which combination best protects it?
options: AES encryption at rest, TLS in transit, RBAC limiting medical fields to the nurse and enrolment officer, audit logging of access
questions.explanation: Sensitive data requires layered controls across confidentiality (encryption + access control), integrity (audit trail) and accountability (logging who viewed what).

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: A developer proposes storing passwords with reversible AES encryption "so we can email them to users who forget". The best critique is:
options: Passwords must be hashed and salted, never reversibly encrypted — a recovery flow should reset, not reveal, the password
questions.explanation: If the system can read the password, so can anyone who compromises the key. Weak credential recovery is explicitly named in OWASP's identification and authentication failures.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: A team adds MFA but leaves session IDs in the URL. The residual risk is:
options: Session hijacking, because the session identifier is exposed and reusable regardless of how strongly the user authenticated
questions.explanation: MFA protects the login; it does nothing once a valid session token is leaked. Controls must cover the whole session lifecycle.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: Which pair of controls is most appropriate for a public comment field?
options: Server-side sanitisation plus output encoding, with a Content Security Policy as defence in depth
questions.explanation: The threat is stored XSS. Sanitising on input and encoding on output means even a missed payload cannot execute, and CSP limits what could run if both fail.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: An organisation runs a pen test once, passes, and takes no further action for three years. The best criticism is:
options: A pen test is a snapshot at one point in time — new code, new components and new attack techniques all create fresh exposure
Vulnerability assessments should never be used
Pen tests must be run daily
questions.explanation: Continuous controls — SAST in the pipeline, dependency scanning, monitoring and periodic reassessment — are what maintain security between tests.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: An application shows "Invalid username" and "Invalid password" as separate messages. This is a weakness because:
options: It confirms to an attacker which usernames exist, aiding credential stuffing
questions.explanation: Username enumeration. A single generic "Invalid username or password" denies the attacker that information — an application of minimal error messaging.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: Which control set best addresses availability for an online exam platform on exam day?
options: Load balancing, autoscaling, rate limiting, CDN, redundancy and a tested failover, with an RTO agreed in advance
questions.explanation: The threat model on exam day is load and outage, not data theft — the controls must match the actual risk.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: A supplier ships a library with a known critical vulnerability. The most appropriate response is:
options: Ignore it if the feature is unused
Patch or replace the component promptly, and add dependency scanning to the pipeline so future issues are detected automatically
questions.explanation: "Vulnerable and outdated components" persists because teams do not know what versions they run — an automated inventory and scan is the systemic fix.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: Which statement best demonstrates the evaluate verb on a security control?
options: "Against the criteria of breach reduction and usability, MFA is justified — it defeats credential stuffing, the dominant attack on this system — though it adds friction and requires an accessible alternative for users who cannot receive codes; on balance it should be mandatory for staff and optional for customers."
"MFA uses something you know and something you have."
questions.explanation: Criteria stated, evidence weighed both ways, limitation acknowledged, judgement made. Definitions alone are 1-mark answers.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: Across a single stimulus system, the strongest analytical move is to:
options: Identify one vulnerability and describe it thoroughly
Recognise that a real system usually has several distinct vulnerabilities, and address each with a matched countermeasure linked to the specific stimulus
questions.explanation: Never assume a stimulus tests only one concept — and generic, technically correct answers that ignore the stimulus are the single most-cited marker complaint.
